clue.text: A chapter of The Prisoner of Zenda? Not likely!

parts.note: a chapter is just some of a book, a portion rather than the whole
The Prisoner of Zenda is the novel by Anthony Hope, so the book stands for its author's surname

explanation.surface: A reader is asked whether one chapter of a classic adventure novel will do, and scoffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel stands for its author, Anthony Hope, so a chapter of it is 'some' of Hope; the whole phrase is an exclamation of scepticism.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironic exclamation meaning there is no chance at all, the same as scoffing 'fat chance!'

clue.text: Taking part of a short track

explanation.surface: Someone takes part of a short railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link. 'Taking part' means taking someone's part, supporting a side.
explanation.definitionFit: Siding with someone is supporting them in an argument; a siding is a short stretch of railway beside the main line.

clue.text: A total failure, this bid

parts.note: in solo whist one bid is a contract to lose every trick, so total failure is the aim

explanation.surface: An attempt is dismissed as a complete flop.
explanation.definitionFit: In solo whist, this declaration commits a player to taking no tricks at all.

clue.text: Fabric that is harsh or rough

indicators.note: rough treatment knocks the letters out of shape and into a new order

parts.note: ie, id est, is the abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: A cloth is described as harsh or coarse to touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' rearranges HARSH, OR and IE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth woven from the mane and tail fibres of the animal was used for upholstery and stiffening.

clue.text: Bowl with spin in this game

parts.note: to pitch is to throw or bowl a ball
and means with, in addition to
to toss a coin is to spin it in the air

explanation.surface: A cricketer bowls with spin in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitch-and-toss is an old gambling game: coins are pitched at a mark and the nearest player tosses them all, keeping those landing heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin-throwing gambling game played in the street, named for its two actions.

clue.text: Profession has run rapidly out of control

explanation.surface: Someone's working life has spiralled away from them.
explanation.definitionFit: A career is one's working life or calling; to career is to rush headlong, swerving wildly like a runaway vehicle.

clue.text: Where adders slide to and fro?

definitions.text: Where adders slide to and fro?

parts.words: Where adders slide to and fro
parts.note: adders are not snakes but people adding up, sliding counting beads back and forth on frames

explanation.surface: A question about where snakes slither back and forth.
explanation.definitionFit: Counting frames with beads on wires are where those doing sums slide the beads.

clue.text: Seaport offering limited right of admission to vessel

indicators.note: limited means cut short, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: an entree is the right to enter or be admitted
a pot is a container or vessel

explanation.surface: A harbour grants restricted access to a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limited' trims ENTREE to ENTRE. 'vessel' looks like a ship but is a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrepot is a port where goods are brought for import and re-export, a trading harbour.

clue.text: Have another think about seas breaking over the ship

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so the earlier letters sit on top of the ship

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: seas breaking like waves are broken up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: Waves crash over a vessel and someone reconsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' looks like waves crashing but signals a rearrangement; in a down entry 'over' means the rearranged seas sit above the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassess is to evaluate again, to reconsider a judgment.

clue.text: Separate here, careful to avoid embarrassment by hearsay

indicators.note: hearsay is what is passed on by word of mouth, so the word is taken as heard rather than as spelt

parts.note: someone discreet is tactful, careful not to cause embarrassment

explanation.surface: A gossip is told to be tactful and keep separate the rumours heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' is only a link. The two words share a sound: the tactful one ends -EET, the one meaning distinct ends -ETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrete things are distinct and individually separate, like the digits on a counter.

clue.text: A sacred word in entrance to Marabar Caves

indicators.note: the entrance is the front of the word, so only its opening letter is taken

parts.note: antra is the plural of antrum, a Latin and anatomical word for a cavity or cave

explanation.surface: A holy syllable echoes at the mouth of the Marabar Caves, as in Forster's A Passage to India.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marabar Caves are from E. M. Forster's A Passage to India, whose echo famously reduces every sound to one syllable. ANTRA is the Latin plural of antrum, a cave or cavity.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or syllable repeated in meditation or prayer, such as Om, is a holy chant of this kind.

clue.text: Foot trouble makes defeated bowmen run away near the end

parts.note: fallen means defeated or overthrown

indicators.note: away says take it out, and near the end says which of the two such letters goes: the one close to the finish

parts.note: archers are bowmen
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Beaten archers flee late in the battle with sore feet.
explanation.walkthrough: ARCHERS has two Rs; the one near the end runs away, leaving ARCHES.
explanation.definitionFit: Collapsed arches of the foot, or flat feet, are a common podiatric complaint.

clue.text: "And always keep a hold of —" (Belloc)

definitions.text: And always keep a hold of

parts.words: And always keep a hold of
parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing: Hilaire Belloc's cautionary verse about Jim warns a child to cling to the woman looking after him, for fear of finding something worse

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash where the missing word goes; the solver completes Belloc's line from 'Jim, who ran away from his Nurse, and was eaten by a Lion'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Belloc's verse the person the child should cling to is the woman employed to look after him, a children's carer.

clue.text: I am betwixt two capes — what excitement!

indicators.note: betwixt is an old word for between, so the letter sits between the two headlands

parts.note: a head is a cape or promontory, as in Beachy Head
a ness is a headland, as in Orford Ness or Loch Ness's neighbours

explanation.surface: Someone stands between two headlands and exclaims at the thrill of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'am' is only a link: just the I sits between. Both capes are words for a headland found in English place names, like Beachy Head and Orford Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: Headiness is the exhilarating, intoxicating quality of something thrilling, a giddy elation.

clue.text: Swaggering characters rousing Viola

indicators.note: the letters, or characters, of the words that follow are taken and rearranged into new order

explanation.surface: Boastful actors stir up Viola, the heroine of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' looks like the cast of a play alongside Viola, but it points to the letters of ROUSING VIOLA, which are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Vainglorious means boastfully proud and conceited, given to swagger and showing off.

clue.text: Raise more contributions for a musical

indicators.note: the words give their letters as contributions toward a new arrangement, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A fundraiser appeals for more donations to stage a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contributions for' signals that RAISE MORE is rearranged. Rose-Marie is a 1924 operetta by Friml and Stothart.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose-Marie is a 1920s operetta set in the Canadian Rockies, a stage show with songs.

clue.text: Surprise sort of university place?

parts.note: Aston, in Birmingham, is home to Aston University
ish is a suffix meaning sort of or somewhat

explanation.surface: Someone wonders, surprised, what kind of place a university is.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston is a district of Birmingham, England, with its own university.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish is to amaze or take aback, a strong synonym.

clue.text: He takes no notice of a country's customs when he travels

definitions.text: He takes no notice of a country's customs when he travels

parts.words: He takes no notice of a country's customs when he travels
parts.note: customs reads as local traditions a rude tourist ignores, but means the customs authorities whose duties he evades

explanation.surface: An ignorant traveller disregards the local ways abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who carries contraband across borders evades the customs officers and their duties.

clue.text: Helping those in despair is a Martinmas resolution

indicators.note: resolution is taken as breaking the words down and resolving them into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone vows, as a resolution on St Martin's Day, to help people in distress.
explanation.walkthrough: Martinmas is St Martin's feast on 11 November. The Samaritans are a British charity that answers calls from people in despair.
explanation.definitionFit: Samaritanism is the practice of helping people in need, after the parable of the Good Samaritan and the British helpline charity.

clue.text: Had accepted short part in "1066 and All That"

indicators.note: accepted means taken in, so the first word receives the other piece
short means cut off before the end, losing the final letter

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: Someone took a small role in a stage version of the comic history book.
explanation.walkthrough: 1066 and All That is a comic British history book; 1066 is the year the English king fell at the Battle of Hastings, so he appears in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The English king killed at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 is a figure in the comic history book.

clue.text: Necklace in stock

explanation.surface: A necklace is kept in a shop's stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. A stock here is an old-fashioned stiff neckcloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-fitting necklace hugs the throat; a stock is a high band of cloth worn tightly round the neck, as is this.

clue.text: Dubious gains invested in gold sovereign by fixer

indicators.note: invested is used as put inside, the way money is put into something

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

indicators.note: something dubious is questionable or shaky, so these letters are not to be trusted in their order

explanation.surface: A shady fixer puts questionable profits into gold coins.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also a British gold coin, which the surface plays on; here it is the monarch, and gold is the heraldic word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixer is someone who arranges and coordinates things, a planner who makes events happen.

clue.text: Post for a rail supporter

explanation.surface: A fence post is used to hold up a rail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the post at the top or foot of a staircase, which holds up the banister handrail.

clue.text: County participating in big time athletics

indicators.note: the answer takes part in the following words, sitting inside them across a word break

explanation.surface: A county takes part in major athletics events.
explanation.walkthrough: Meath is a county in the Republic of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Meath is one of the counties of Ireland, in the province of Leinster.

clue.text: The sort of relations created by unions

definitions.text: The sort of relations created by unions

parts.words: The sort of relations created by unions
parts.note: unions sounds like trade unions and industrial relations, but means marriages, which bring with them family members by marriage

explanation.surface: Trade unions shape industrial relations.
explanation.definitionFit: Marriage makes a spouse's parents and siblings into family members by marriage.

clue.text: Wild flower, good for cleaner hair

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British word for a cleaning lady
a lock is a tress or curl of hair

explanation.surface: A wild plant is recommended as a good hair rinse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good for' is only a link. CHAR is a dated British word for a woman who cleans houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlock is wild mustard, a yellow-flowered weed of fields and waysides.

clue.text: Mother's lad maybe sings like such an angel

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman, so mother's lad is her lad

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be otherwise, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mother's son perhaps sings like an angel in the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: The angel is from the carol 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing', which is why such an angel sings.
explanation.definitionFit: In the carol the angels announcing the birth are messengers bearing tidings, which is what this word means.

clue.text: A climber beginning to belay, for example

explanation.surface: A mountaineer starts by securing the rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'belay' is a climbing term for securing a rope, which supports the first reading. In typography the start of belay, the letter b, rises above the line, as do d, h, k and l.
explanation.definitionFit: One who goes up is a climber; in printing, a tall lowercase letter such as b, whose stroke rises above the others, has the same name.
